title: Teaching himself bass and Wellman Braud's advice on tone
summary: Violin made bass easy to learn; Braud taught him to keep fingers down for full note value.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Bass players: lineage, tone and technique

blocks.x: That's interesting. Well, you said that when things got too rough musically, you'd go back to tuba to play the parts. Did you study string bass with anybody? Or how did --
Only my --
How did you develop as such a fine bass player?

Well, it was easier for me to learn string bass, on account of the violin. All I had to do was learn the fingering, the positions. Which is, you know, it's a little different. But it just seemed natural to me, just like the small violin. So it didn't take me long after -- oh, about two, three weeks, I could do pretty good on the string bass, you know, and I didn't have to change.
You just taught yourself?
Yeah.

You've always gotten a very beautiful dark sound on string bass. And I've noticed other bass players that have come out of Chicago have this dark tone. I'm now speaking of the sound of the tone. Did you strive for that, or do you feel that was just -- came out naturally
the way you played? William (Wellman) Braud was sponsoring me playing like I'm playing. Used to be with Duke. Duke's first bass player.
Right.

He's the one that taught me how to pick and hold -- told me I had to keep my fingers down tight on the fingerboard. You can't do like that -- when you put your fingers down on a string bass, you've got to put your fingers down and keep it down there while you're picking. To give the note the full value, you understand? Otherwise it would be just plucking like.
Right. Staccato.
Yeah. So he was responsible for that.
Well, how did you get together with Wellman Braud?

Well, when we played theaters. Sometimes like when I was at the Regal Theater with Dave Peyton, Duke Ellington's band played on the stage. They had a week there. And I got together with Braud. And then everytime he'd come into town, when I was at the Grand Terrace, he'd come by.
Did he teach you his slapping technique? Some of the records that he did with --
Yeah, well, I was doing that a long time before I met him. That's the only way I could get off
on string bass, because there was a lot of slapping going on back in them days.
Was that a novelty effect?
Yeah, that finally went out.
Except with Milt Hinton.
Yeah, he still slaps?
Oh, yeah, an awful lot. Takes solo, do a slap solo. Do a double slap. I was playing with him one time, I said, can you do a triple slap, and he did.
Yeah.
